309. **Maintenance mode — `settings.json > server.maintenance` (#MAINT1, shipped in 0.6.10).** A bundle can be closed to the public without being stopped: when maintenance is active every request EXCEPT the `/_gina/*` family is answered `503` + `Retry-After` + `Cache-Control: no-store` with a self-contained maintenance page (HTML for a browser navigation, the shipped `{error:{code:'503',message:'GNA:GLOBAL:ERR:503',explicit:<message>}}` body for XHR / `X-Gina-Navigate` / json-only `Accept`). Config: `{enabled:false, retryAfter:300, message, bypassKey, allowFrom:[]}` — `enabled` must be a STRICT boolean, every other key falls back PER KEY with a boot warning, and a malformed block never refuses a boot (the `server.transientErrors` lint contract). **Placement is the feature, and it is why a route middleware cannot substitute:** the gate sits AFTER every `/_gina/*` handler and BEFORE the webroot filter, static-asset serving, both render/output-cache serve points and routing. Middleware only runs once a route has MATCHED, so a middleware-based maintenance mode leaves static assets serving 200 and answers 404 (not 503) for any unmatched URL; a cache serve point above a gate replays cached pages to the public. `/_gina/*` staying reachable is deliberate: `/_gina/health/check` keeps answering 200 so an orchestrator does not restart pods over a declared window (correct k8s maintenance keeps pods READY and serves the 503 from the app — this feature deliberately does NOT flip readiness, which would make the ingress return connection errors instead of your page; a probe that targets an APPLICATION route instead sits below the gate and must present `x-gina-maintenance-key` from the probe's own headers, on EVERY such probe — a failing liveness or startup probe makes the kubelet restart the container — with `bypassKey` in settings before the window opens (config-only; the runtime toggle cannot add it)), and the operator can always reach the toggle. Cost when off is one property read plus a boolean. **Bypass — the key is topology-independent, the IP list is not.** `bypassKey` is compared in constant time (`crypto.timingSafeEqual`, length-guarded, fail-closed when unset) and may be presented as the `x-gina-maintenance-key` header (programmatic callers) or once as `?gina-maintenance-key=…` in a browser, which mints a stateless `<expUnix>.<HMAC-SHA256>` cookie (`gina.maintenance`, 12h, HttpOnly/SameSite=Lax/Path=/, `Secure` on https) and 302s to the same URL WITHOUT the secret — the `Location` is the stripped PATH ONLY, never rebuilt from `Host` or any `X-Forwarded-*` header, since a redirect target built from attacker-controlled headers is an open redirect. Verification recomputes the MAC, so a grant survives a restart and works across every bundle of a merged-mode project sharing the key with nothing to replicate; rotating `bypassKey` revokes every outstanding cookie. `allowFrom` is honoured **ONLY for requests that do NOT classify as proxied** (the `request._ginaIsProxyHost` stamp when present, else the same port-less-Host-OR-`X-Forwarded-Host` heuristic, `server.proxy.requireForwardedHeaders` respected): behind a reverse proxy every `req.socket.remoteAddress` is the PROXY's, so an unconditioned IP allowlist would either admit the entire internet (proxy listed) or nobody (proxy not listed) — the condition turns that silent-open into fail-closed and leaves the key as the bypass that works under any topology. Resolution order: cookie → header → query(+grant) → IP∧¬proxied → 503. An invalid presented key is logged once, never with its value. **Runtime toggle:** `GET/POST /_gina/maintenance` (always-on, admin-gated on `app.json > admin.allowFrom`, both engines, declared ABOVE the gate so the off switch is never stranded behind it). `POST {"enable":true|false[,"ttlSeconds":N,"retryAfter":N,"message":"…"]}`; the status payload reports `hasBypassKey` but NEVER the key. A runtime override is NOT persisted — a restart returns the bundle to its configured state, and an expired `ttlSeconds` reverts to CONFIG rather than to "off", so a forgotten dead-man timer can never re-open a site `settings.json` says is closed. `enabled:true` in config is the durable form. **`ttlSeconds` is an INTEGER in 1..86400 (24h) and a PRESENT value outside that is refused 400 naming the bound and the config alternative (#B498, 0.6.28) — until then any invalid ttl (25h, a float, a numeric string) was SILENTLY ignored and the flip applied with NO timer, i.e. an unbounded window when a bounded one was asked for, `until: null` the only tell; absent or `null` still mean "no timer". Refused rather than clamped on purpose: a shorter-than-asked maintenance window reopens a site mid-deploy, so there is no safe direction to round toward (the instrument window clamps because a shorter CAPTURE window is harmless).** Scope is per BUNDLE: state lives on the engine instance and a server serves exactly one bundle, so merged-process mode gets per-bundle isolation for free. **Verified scope of the "every request except `/_gina/*`" claim:** the gate is pinned on the engine-agnostic `onRequest()` path (express) and the isaac request listener, above statics, both render/output-cache serve points and routing. **The contract holds under HTTP/2, MEASURED (#B383, resolved 2026-08-16) — and the reason is a CONSTRAINT that binds every future pre-routing gate: the gate must be SYNCHRONOUS.** Node's compat layer registers its own `'stream'` listener when a `'request'` listener attaches, so `core/server.js`'s separate raw byte-serving `onHttp2Strem` — registered lazily from inside the first h2 static request, and therefore SECOND on the same emitter — runs only after the compat listener returns. Because EventEmitter dispatches synchronously in registration order, a synchronous gate completes its 503 while the compat listener still holds the stack. An ASYNC gate (`await`, callback, promise, `setImmediate`) yields to the emitter first and the raw listener then serves the asset underneath it: measured as a 200 BYPASS in a 6-arm micro-replica whose synchronous arm held at 503, with a positive control serving 200. Live h2 boot confirmed statics/routed/unmatched all 503 while `/_gina/health/check` stayed 200, plus one harmless `ERR_HTTP2_HEADERS_SENT` (gina's listener losing the race it was always going to lose) which `lib/proc` downgrades to a warn — the bundle stays up. ws UPGRADEs are deliberately out of scope in slice 1 (existing sockets survive a window). Server-side only — `lib/maintenance` is absent from the browser `build.json`, so pickup is a bundle RESTART, no re-bake.

310. **`Collection.replace()` resolves its comparison key from BOTH sides — the stored entry AND the caller's `set` (#B393, gh issue #64, shipped in 0.6.11).** `replace(filter, set[, key])` locates each entry to overwrite by comparing a key on the stored row against the same key on `set`. That key used to be chosen by inspecting the STORED row alone: it defaulted to the internal `_uuid`, fell back to `id` only when the stored row had no `_uuid`, and threw `No comparison key defined !` only in that same stored-row-lacks-it case. So the one combination neither branch covered — **stored row HAS `_uuid`, `set` does NOT** — compared `<storedUuid> == undefined`, which is never true: nothing matched, nothing was replaced, no error was raised, and the call returned a chainable result that looked successful. A silent, lossy write. Reachability is the non-obvious part: a Collection built from fresh raw data keeps no `_uuid` on the instance rows, so the `id` fallback fires and the call works — the defect appears only once the caller has **re-loaded an array a previous chained call returned**, because chained results carry the internal `_uuid` on every row the call did not replace (and `toRaw()` KEEPS a `_uuid` the caller supplied, since the constructor stamps `_hasItsOwnUuid` on reload). That is why it presents as intermittent rather than constant, and why persisting a chained result is the trigger. Now: the key is resolved per entry from both sides, falling back to `id` when BOTH carry one, and refusing loudly when the two sides share no usable key — so the previously-silent combination is no longer the quiet one. An explicitly supplied `key` argument is honoured exactly as before (no fallback, no refusal). The resolved key is also scoped per entry instead of assigned to the shared variable, so a fallback taken for one row can no longer apply to rows examined after it. Every previously-working shape is unchanged, including `set` carrying a matching `_uuid` and the fresh-collection `id` path. **`lib/collection` IS in the browser `build.json`, so pickup is a bundle RESTART **and** a re-bake.**

311. **Per-call identity for concurrent entity calls — the ENTITY layer pairs each emit to the call it came from by AsyncLocalStorage identity (#B440, 0.6.20 — SECURITY; it was FIFO-paired from #B394 in 0.6.11 until then), the COUCHBASE CONNECTOR layer settles per call (#B429/#B430/#B431, 0.6.19). Two different mechanisms; do not reason from one to the other.** ⚠️ The description below covers ONLY hand-written entity methods that call `self.emit('<shortName>#<method>')` — and registration is a SOURCE-TEXT scan (`entity.js` tests `entity[prop].toString()` for the literal, comments INCLUDED): a comment that merely names the trigger registers the method, passing the trigger name to a helper registers it, and removing the last occurrence un-registers it (plain function: no wrapper, no `.onComplete()`, no Promise return — a call-contract change for its callers). Methods generated from `.sql` files never reach it — `core/model/entity.js:349-351`/`:414-417` say so verbatim (the connector emits the PREFIXED `N1QL:entity#method`, the entity buffer listens on the unprefixed name), so their guarantees come from the connector, described at the end of this entry. **Entity layer (`core/model/entity.js`):** The `util.promisify` fast-path (taken when a method is called detached — `this[m]` undefined + trailing function arg) used to back its pending callback into a SCALAR slot (`entity._callbacks[shortName] = cb`) plus a per-call `.once` guarded on that slot. Two concurrent calls on the SAME method raced on the one slot: the second overwrote the first, the first-arriving result was flushed to the LAST-registered callback (cross-delivery — caller B receives caller A's record), and the displaced caller's `.once` found its guard false so its promise NEVER settled (starvation — a hung request, nothing logged; the write-path variant silently persists A's document under B's key). Option B (entity-context calls) had already been given a FIFO queue + one persistent `.on` dispatcher (#M2); the fast-path kept the scalar because its own comment claimed it "bypasses queue". Now it uses the same shape: push each invocation's callback onto `entity._callbacks[shortName]` (an array), register ONE persistent `_onFpQueueEmit` dispatcher (guarded on `listenerCount === 0`) that shifts the OLDEST callback per emit and removes itself when the queue drains. The custom `emit`'s third guard already routes an ARRAY slot straight to native emit (skips `setListener` when `!Array.isArray`), so the `.on` listener receives the emit args directly. Guarantees after #B394: no callback is ever orphaned by a SIBLING call's overwrite; cross-delivery closed for in-order completion. ⚠️ **#B394's "starvation ELIMINATED" was TOO STRONG, and its documented out-of-order residual was the smaller half of the problem — #B440 (0.6.20, SECURITY): ONE lost emit permanently desynchronised the FIFO.** Both dispatchers paired an emit to the OLDEST queued resolver with no call identity, so a call that never emitted (canonically a throw inside an un-awaited `async` callback BEFORE the emit — swallowed, only `unhandledRejection` sees it) left its resolver at the head forever: with overlapping callers every later caller of that method received the NEXT caller's record and the last one hung; sequential callers all hung; the desync survives dev hot-reload and DEEPENS by one dead resolver per lost emit (measured in a real boot on both call forms: `LOSE→B, B→C, C→D, D HUNG, LATER HUNG`). Same failure shape as #B429 — where the method reads a user-scoped record, an ownership check can pass on another principal's row — hence a Security entry. The trigger is DATA-dependent (an unexpected record shape), not load-dependent: invisible in a load test, inevitable in a long-lived process. **Fix:** every wrapped call runs inside a per-process `AsyncLocalStorage` (`process.gina._entityCallALS`, shared across hot-reload generations) carrying `{ e, r }` (trigger + this call's resolver); both dispatchers call `_dequeueByIdentity(q, e)` — store names THIS trigger ⇒ splice that call's own resolver, or DROP the emit if that call already settled (never hand a late completion to the head: the tempting forget-then-`shift()` variant measurably hands A's late record to B); no store, or another trigger's ⇒ `shift()` in arrival order plus a levelled `DISPATCH:NO_CONTEXT` debug line — the honest boundary, a completion reaching the entity outside every call's async context (e.g. a native driver invoking callbacks from a loop started at boot), measured identical to pre-fix. Resolvers `_forget` themselves on settle while the persistent listener stays, which is what makes a late duplicate emit DROP instead of being buffered into `_arguments` and poisoning the next fast-path call. The fast-path now captures `cached.apply()`'s return and chains `_fpInner.then()` — its old comment claimed an escape via `_innerResult.then()` that exists only in Option B, so a Promise-returning method was immune on Option B and NOT on the fast-path (measured; a consumer's promisify→direct-await conversion was therefore necessary, not belt-and-braces). The fast-path also runs the caller's raw callback inside the store that was active when the call was made, so an entity method that calls another entity's method with a direct callback and emits its own completion from inside it still pairs by identity (measured: without that it fell back to arrival order; `.onComplete`/`.then`/promisify chains pair by identity regardless, because promise continuations keep their context). The #B394 out-of-order residual is CLOSED as a by-product (each own on both forms; `entity-promisify-concurrency.test.js` §03 now pins each-own). **Opt-in bound `settings.json > model.emitTimeout` (ms; absent/0 = no bound, the previous liveness contract; schema + settings reference + Models guide document it):** read once per entity at wrap time via `self.getConfig(self.bundle,'settings')`, it rejects a call that never completes with an Error naming the trigger and `#B440` and logs the same line at warn; set it above the slowest legitimate bulk operation, which is why there is no default. Cost ≈ +3.6 µs/call. Test `test/core/entity-call-identity.test.js` (22 arms across both call forms — lost emit, the bound, a lone later caller, out-of-order, the fast-path Promise chain, late-duplicate drop, callback chain, no-context fallback with its debug line, config read, drain; red-first on the pre-fix bytes through its `B440_ENTITY_SRC` lever: 17 red, the 5 green are the labelled controls). ⚠️ The published Models guide's concurrency note used to promise *"no call is ever left hanging"* — false before #B440 and true only under the bound — and its `insert` example wrapped a synchronous `try/catch` around an asynchronous callback, which cannot catch a throw raised inside that callback: the trigger shape itself. Both corrected in the same release. Framework-internal `promisify` sites (`controller.js` `self.query`, `form-validator.js`) promisify a CONTROLLER method, not an entity trigger, so they never enter this branch (gated on `entity._triggers`). Server-side only — NOT browser-bundled, so pickup is a bundle RESTART, no re-bake. Test `test/core/entity-promisify-concurrency.test.js` (4 arms, bounded-settle so a regression fails rather than hangs; red-first validated against pre-fix bytes — serial control green, the three concurrency arms red; §03 tightened to each-own by #B440). **Couchbase connector layer (`core/connectors/couchbase/index.js`, #B429, 0.6.19 — SECURITY):** the completion trigger `'N1QL:'+entity+'#'+method` carries NO call identity and is emitted on the entity SINGLETON (`EntitySuper[Name].instance`, `entity.js:475-493`), so the Promise/`await`/`.onComplete()` path — which reached `self.once(trigger)` because its `_internalCb` is a function — was settled by a listener EVERY in-flight caller of that method shared. Node fires all listeners on one emit, so the first completion woke them all with ITS payload and removed them: a BROADCAST, **not** arrival-order pairing, so it cross-delivered on IN-ORDER completion too (measured `A→A, B→A`) — strictly worse than the entity-layer residual above, and the reason a confidentiality/authorization concern arises (an ownership read answered with another caller's row). The explicit trailing-callback form was always safe (it settles from `onQueryCallback`'s own closure). **Fix:** the Promise path assigns `_mainCallback = _internalCb` so BOTH forms settle through one per-call `_deliver()` guard; `register()` collapses to a single dispatch and `_isRegisteredFromProto` is retired (measured inert — reset every invocation, and `register` has no `await`, so it never actually starved a query); the early error emit is gone; ONE emit per completion remains, deliberately, because `entity.js`'s emit override forwards an `N1QL:*`-matched trigger to `lib/inspector-events` (verified live) — a side effect is that the bridge now also sees direct-callback completions it previously missed. `bulkInsert` carried the same defect independently (its own trigger + `once`) and is fixed the same way. **`bulkInsert` also carried a SECOND, unrelated defect that #B429 did not reach — #B460 (0.6.24): its outer `try` wraps its OWN function body, so a synchronous throw in the prologue was caught, `console.error`d and swallowed, and the method fell off the end returning `undefined`.** Both documented shapes broke on that path: the `await` form (its own docblock's first `@example`) resolved with `undefined` — a caller treating "did not throw" as success recorded an insert that never happened — and `.onComplete(cb)` threw a TypeError on `undefined`; in both, the error existed only in the log and was unreachable to the caller. ⚠️ **The trigger is NOT only a cluster outage:** the prologue carries two DELIBERATE argument validations (`rec` falsy; a record without `.values`) whose errors the author wrote to reach the caller, which makes the defect reproducible with no cluster at all — `entity.bulkInsert(undefined)` is a complete repro, and that is what makes it testable without the SDK. **Fix:** the promise, its one-shot `_settle` resolver and the `.onComplete` shim are built BEFORE the try, so the catch settles this call (`_settle(err); return _promise;`) — `.onComplete(cb)` receives `(err)`, the `await` form rejects, and `_settle`'s `_settled` latch means a late throw cannot double-settle. ⚠️ **SCOPE — the fix moves the RETURN axis only, not the SETTLED-VALUE axis, and conflating them is what a consumer will do:** the success handler still runs `if (!_data || _data.length == 0) { _data = null }` and only promotes an error when `_meta.errors` is present, so a rows-less success reaches `_settle(false, null, _meta)` and RESOLVES WITH `null`. A non-rejection therefore still does NOT prove rows were inserted — a rows-based success check remains load-bearing after the fix (measured with a consumer whose guard was written against the pre-fix `undefined`). Generalises: after fixing a settlement defect, say which of the two axes moved — what the function RETURNS synchronously, vs what its promise RESOLVES WITH — because any downstream guard or comment written against the untouched axis keeps its conclusion while its stated premise goes stale. ⚠️ **Behaviour change: a fire-and-forget call that ignores the return now surfaces an `unhandledRejection`** where it previously failed silently (gna.js logs it, never responds) — deliberate, and documented in the migration guide. **The QUERY path does NOT share this shape and needed no change:** its promise is built inside `entities[entityName].prototype[name] = function(){…}`, an ATTACHED method, so the enclosing try has already exited by call time and a throw propagates to the caller normally — `bulkInsert` is the only method whose try wraps its own body. Generalises: **a `try` that wraps a whole promise-returning function body must settle in its `catch`, or the contract silently inverts on the failure path** — and the plumbing it settles through has to be constructed OUTSIDE that try, or it is still `undefined` when the catch runs. Tests: `test/core/couchbase-connector.test.js §14` (6 arms over EXTRACT-AND-EXECUTED shipped bytes — both call shapes driven through the real validation throws, plus three controls that are green pre-fix: the extraction anti-vacuity, the happy path reaching `resolveCluster().query()`, and the query-path-is-different pin; red-first measured 3 red / 3 green). **Siblings found while fixing it:** #B430 — the delivery `catch` re-invoked a THROWING caller callback with the same payload (ran it twice); #B431 — all three dispatches chained `.catch(onError).then(onResult)`, and a `.catch()` returning normally RESOLVES, so the trailing `.then()` ran on EVERY error and settled a second time with a bogus empty success (measured: `(Error,null,undefined)` then `(false,null,{})`, so `if (err) return next(err); render(data)` ran BOTH branches; invisible on the await path because a promise settles once, but it is why a failed query emitted 3×). Now `.then(onResult, onError)` — mutually exclusive branches — at all three sites. **Scope, PER DEFECT — the `.once(`/`.emit(` count scopes #B429 ONLY** (it requires a shared emitter; #B430/#B431 involve none, so that instrument is structurally blind to them — an over-scoped 'couchbase only' was relayed on 2026-08-27 and retracted the same day). **#B429: couchbase ONLY** — the other six ORM connectors settle on a per-call native Promise and use the trigger for debug/inspector logging only (`.once(`/`.emit(` = 0 in each, 12 in couchbase). **#B431: couchbase ONLY, verified with a PAREN-MATCHING scanner** (a character-window regex false-positived twice by spanning `});`+`return`+`else` into a different statement's `.then`) — validated against the pre-fix file as a known positive: 3 there, 0 across all nine connectors now. **#B430's class IS present elsewhere — triaged 2026-08-28 as #B432, and the count is 53, not the ~20 the first pass suggested.** A caller's callback is application code and throws for ordinary reasons (a template error, a null deref in a handler); two shapes then ran it a SECOND time with a different payload — the sync `try { cb(null, rows); } catch (e) { cb(e); }`, and the mirror `.then(function(){ cb(null, rows); }).catch(function(e){ cb(e); })`, whose trailing catch is reached when the SUCCESS handler throws. Both deliver a success and then an error for one operation (so `if (err) { return next(err); } render(data);` runs BOTH branches) and the second call reports the caller's own exception as a database failure. ⚠️ **Four instrument corrections, each of which had produced a wrong reading:** (1) a hand-written settle-name list MISSES the real callbacks — derive them per file (a param that is invoked, an `args.pop()` capture, a resolver binding); the stores settle through `fn`, and 35 sites hid behind a `0`. (2) A settle reached through a LOCAL HELPER is invisible without a fixpoint pass (`attempt`, `runQuery`, `withCollection`). (3) A lexical try/catch pair is NOT a defect when the settle sits in a nested async callback (its throw never reaches the enclosing sync catch — this alone cleared mysql, postgresql and duckdb) nor when an inner `try/catch` swallows it first, nor when the trailing settle lives in a SIBLING `else` branch. (4) A native promise resolver settles once, so a double settle through `_resolve`/`_reject` is BENIGN — 7 of 60 findings. Validate any such scanner on the pre-fix couchbase file as a known positive (it must report the #B430 site and both #B431 sites) and on the post-fix file (0). **Measured clean, both directions: mysql, postgresql, duckdb, ai** (`ai` has no callback path at all — only a native resolver). **FIXED in the entity dispatch path (0.6.19):** `core/connectors/settle-once.js` — a dependency-free sibling of `param-redact`/`sql-parser` exposing `settleOnce(label, cb, reporter)`, which returns a PER-CALL guard that delivers at most once, forwards any arity, and reports a callback throw (tagged with the query trigger) instead of replaying it. ⚠️ Build it per invocation, never at module scope — a module-scope guard would let the FIRST call suppress every later one. Wired at sqlite (`node:sqlite` is synchronous, so its callback ran inside the `try` with no microtask boundary — the most reachable instance of the whole class), mongodb (callback dispatch AND the unknown-op branch, which is reachable because `op` is validated only for falsiness, never against the recognised list) and scylladb. `couchbase/index.js` keeps its own inline `_deliver()` — the reference implementation this module generalises. **Store layers — the same shape with framework-supplied callbacks, fixed at METHOD ENTRY** by rebinding (`fn = settleOnce(label, fn, console)` immediately after the `fn = noop` normalization), so every settle path in the method — nested try/catch AND promise chain — funnels through one guard: **session stores** (couchbase v3/v4, mongodb, redis, scylladb, sqlite — 30 methods) and the **async-job stores** (mongodb, sqlite — 10 methods). ⚠️ **A LEXICAL scanner still reports these files HARMFUL, and that is CORRECT-and-expected, not a regression** — the fix REBINDS `fn` rather than renaming call sites, so the matched `fn(...)`-in-try-plus-catch shape is unchanged. A syntactic scanner's post-fix reading is evidence ONLY when the fix changed the syntax it matches; when it rebinds, the verification burden moves entirely to behavioural coverage (`connector-settle-parity.test.js` §05/§06, one arm per store over EXTRACT-AND-EXECUTED shipped bytes plus a wrap census pinning method-count == wrap-count per file). **Connector open paths (`mongodb`/`scylladb` `lib/connector.js` `onReady`) — FIXED, wrapped CONDITIONALLY** (`if (typeof fn === 'function') fn = settleOnce(…)`; measured: an unconditional wrap turns a missing callback from a loud `fn is not a function` rejection into a silent boot hang). The handler is `core/model/index.js`'s `connect` continuation; measured through the real bytes of both, a throwing continuation was re-invoked with a fabricated `Connection failed: <its own message>` AND the connector registry cache was overwritten to `err=<fabricated>, conn=null`, served to every later `connect()` for the process life — now 1 invocation, `err=null`, cache intact, the exception reported under `<connector>:connector#onReady`. The sqlite `inspector#indexes` listener is guarded for consistency (its `_ixCollector` caller has no throwing path; if it ever did, the double decrement would answer `/_gina/indexes` early with partial data). **Couchbase storage-store — CONVERTED to the shared guard** (its own local `once()` already prevented the double settle — measured on all 9 verbs with a firing subtract-control — but its JSDoc claim that the exception 'surfaces as an unhandled rejection' was FALSE on all nine: six verbs lost it silently, three (`stats`/`listZeroRefs`/`listKeys`) logged it misattributed as `<verb> failed`); now 9 wraps at verb entry (`couchbase:storage#<verb>`, reporter = the file's own global `console`), the exception reported once and never entering the CAS-retry / `withCollection` catches. The `once`→`settleOnce` swap is inert for callers: no consumer of any verb's return value exists (measured), and every strategy closure opens `if (err) return fn(err)`. **Every one of the 53 triaged sites is now guarded — the class is CLOSED** (4 entity-dispatch + 24 session-store + 10 job-store + 5 connector-open/Inspector + 10 storage-store). Test `test/core/connector-settle-parity.test.js` (one contract declared ONCE and run against every fixed connector, plus a deliberately UNGUARDED replica that must fail the discriminating arms — without it a spec every backend passes could be a spec asserting nothing; red-first measured 11 pass / 19 fail pre-fix, with every green in the code-the-fix-does-not-change bucket). Server-side only, pickup = bundle RESTART, no re-bake. Test `test/core/couchbase-concurrency.test.js` (25 arms booting the REAL connector against a controllable cluster stub so completion ORDER is chosen not raced; callback arms CAPTURE every invocation behind a grace window so a double settle is observable; red-first validated — 16 red pre-fix, and the arms that stay GREEN pre-fix are exactly the controls: serial, explicit-callback, mixed-form-no-starvation, success paths, the Inspector bridge). **#B441 (0.6.30, SECURITY) — a completion emitted AFTER its call settled is discarded at the entity's `emit`, never buffered for the next caller.** Both dispatchers remove themselves once their queue drains, so when a method emits its completion trigger more than once per call (once per loop iteration, for instance) the first emit settles the caller correctly and every SURPLUS emit finds no listener and takes the legacy `setListener` buffering path into `entity._arguments`; the fast-path's next detached caller then consumed that entry as its own result (`DISPATCH:BUFFER_CALLBACK`), the caller after it too, and the buffer grew by one entry per surplus emit — measured on a built prod release (B and C both received A's record, `_arguments` 2→4→6). Entity-context callers were immune (the #M5 per-call clear), and DEV MODE MASKS IT COMPLETELY (`isCacheless` runs the same clear on every wrapped call), so a local dev reproduction reading clean is not evidence. Fix: `_forget` — the single choke point of every settle path (identity dispatch, returned Promise, `model.emitTimeout`) — stamps the resolver `_settled`; the `emit` override reads the active per-call store and, when it names this trigger and its resolver is settled, marks the emit SURPLUS: `setListener` is skipped (nothing buffered) and `DISPATCH:REPEAT_EMIT` is logged ONCE per call at the second emit (one late emit after a Promise/timeout settle stays silent — the documented benign shape). `DISPATCH:NO_CONTEXT` moved from `_dequeueByIdentity` to the same emit-time site and now fires pending or not (a zero count used to be ambiguous: the line was gated on a non-empty queue that the self-removed dispatcher never reached). Numbered `<trigger>N` loop variants of the call's own trigger stay silent. The two `listenerCount(trigger) === 0`-after-drain invariants are untouched. Pickup: bundle restart, no re-bake. Test: `test/core/entity-b441-dispatch-signals.test.js` (15 arms; red-first 10 red / 5 controls on the pre-fix bytes via `B440_ENTITY_SRC`).

312. **Every `Collection` method that accepts a filter object refuses undefined-valued filter keys — the silent match-all is closed (#B396, gh issue #65, shipped in 0.6.12).** `find()` round-trips its filter objects through `JSON.stringify(arguments)`/`JSON.parse`, and stringify silently DROPS keys whose value is `undefined` — so `findOne({ id: source.missingId })` degraded to the match-everything `{}` filter and returned the collection's FIRST row (an arbitrary, plausible-looking wrong record), a mixed filter silently lost its undefined constraint, and `update({ id: undefined }, set)` wrote `set` onto EVERY record. The in-loop guard deeper in the matcher (message: ``filter `<key>` cannot be left undefined``) was written to refuse exactly this input but was DEAD CODE — the serialization stripped the keys before the loop could see them (JSON.parse can never produce an `undefined` value). The fix hoists the refusal to `find()`'s entry, BEFORE the round-trip; `findOne`, `or` and `update` all delegate to `find`, so the one gate covers the family. Deliberately unchanged: an explicitly EMPTY `{}` filter still means "no constraint" (match-all), `null` stays a legal needle comparing strictly against stored values (matches stored `null`), array arguments are skipped (record sets, not needles), and `notIn`'s ARRAY form (`notIn(rows, key)`) is unaffected because it skips `find()` entirely. ⚠️ Every OTHER filter-object entry point IS covered, including four this entry originally excluded by mistake: `notIn({…})` routes a filter-object argument straight into `find()` (`main.js:869`), `delete()` is a pure delegation to `notIn()` (`:1297`), and `replace()` (`:1199`) and `max()` (`:1373`) call `find()` too — so the covered family is EIGHT entry points, not four. Pre-fix consequences on the four that went undocumented were the worst of the set: `delete({ id: undefined })` returned an EMPTY collection (every record removed — it returns a filtered COPY, so the loss lands in the returned value, not in-place) and `max({ k: undefined })` aggregated over the whole collection instead of the filtered subset. Measured on the published `v0.6.11` vs `v0.6.12` trees with controls; no internal framework caller can pass undefined (two independent sweeps: zero live `notIn`/`replace`/`max` sites, and the two `delete` sites — `lib/proc.js:614`, `core/config.js:2887` — are each structurally string-valued or dominated by an identical-filter `findOne` that throws first). By-catch hardening: the FormValidator's conditional-case rules lookup (`findOne({ case: fields[caseName] })`) could silently merge the FIRST condition's rules when the case field was absent from the form — the refusal now routes that state into the lookup's own designed catch-and-skip (its warn already said "undeclared or misconfigured case"). Behaviour change for consumers relying on undefined-key-means-no-constraint: build filters conditionally (add a key only when its value is defined). ⚠️ That recipe is ONLY for the no-constraint intent — for a LOOKUP BY A POSSIBLY-ABSENT KEY (`if (!col.findOne({id: maybeAbsent}))`, `col.findOne({id: maybeAbsent}) || fallback`) it is the WRONG migration: an empty filter matches everything and returns the FIRST row, so the guard reads "found" and the fallback never runs — measured. Guard the CALL instead: `var row = (id != null) ? col.findOne({id: id}) : null;`. **`lib/collection` IS in the browser `build.json`, so pickup is a bundle RESTART **and** a re-bake.**

313. **Redis is a store backend only — no entity/ORM wiring, by design.** The redis connector class is deliberately empty: it backs FOUR purpose-bound subsystems, each minting its OWN client — the session store (`lib.SessionStore`), the async-job store (`app.json` `jobs.store`), the render-cache L2 (`settings.json` `server.cache` `type: "redis"`), and — since #KV1 slice 1 — a KV namespace backend (`settings.json` `kv.namespaces.<name>.store`; entry 314), one client PER NAMESPACE. Client failure policy diverges per subsystem by design — the render-cache L2 sets `enableOfflineQueue: false` plus a `commandTimeout` so an outage fails page-serving open instead of hanging every request, while the job store keeps ioredis's default offline queue on, and the KV store imposes NEITHER: it passes those knobs through from the `connectors.json` entry so the operator tunes per namespace (a `failMode: "open"` namespace wants the fail-fast trio; a `closed` one usually wants the queue). NON-KV redis use — data structures, pub/sub, third-party queue libraries — stays app-owned by design: it is outside the KV contract, so an app needing it reads its `connectors.json` entry via `getConfig()` and mints its own ioredis client. Redis operations do NOT appear in the Inspector's query log: `_devQueryLog` capture hangs off the entity query path, which this connector deliberately does not implement; a render-cache L2 hit is instead observable per response via the RFC 9211 `Cache-Status` header. Per-operation Inspector capture of redis store traffic was evaluated 2026-08-21 and demand-gated (measured consumer demand: zero); if demand arrives, the evidenced shape is a store-reachability/lifecycle signal on the events channel (with app-registered clients joining the same signal), not query-log wiring.

314. **General-purpose KV primitive (#KV1) — `gina.kv('<namespace>')`, strict-declared namespaces over pluggable per-namespace backends (`settings.json > kv`).** Declare namespaces under `kv.namespaces` (`{ "kv": { "default": "cache", "namespaces": { "cache": { "failMode": "open" }, "tokens": {} } } }`); `gina.kv(name)` THROWS on an unconfigured block or unknown name (the throw is what surfaces a typo — the `gina.storage()` stance), and the whole feature is dormant when the block is absent. Namespaces are process-global, read once at boot from the STARTING bundle's settings. The handle is promise-native with 13 ops: `get` / `set(k, v, {ttl})` / `del` / `has` / `ttl(k)` (null=miss, -1=no expiry, else remaining ms) / `expire(k, ttlMs)` / `setnx` (set-if-absent) / `consume` (atomic read-AND-delete — the one-shot-token op; the second reader gets null) / `incr` / `decr` (integer counters; `{ttl}` applies on CREATE only; non-integer values and safe-range overflow reject) / `delIfEquals` (compare-and-delete — the safe lock-release primitive; compose with `setnx` for lock recipes) / `clear()` / `getOrSet(k, {ttl}, loader)` (fetch-or-compute with per-process single-flight; no negative caching). Value model: JSON-serialized; `undefined` AND `null` are REFUSED on every write (a stored null would be indistinguishable from a miss — store a wrapper or use `del()`); TTLs are MILLISECONDS, positive integers only — `ttl: 0` refuses rather than meaning no-expiry. Per-namespace `failMode`: `closed` (default) rejects on backend errors; `open` degrades every op to its miss-shaped result with a warning (cache-like namespaces) — consulted on backend errors only, so it becomes operative with connector-backed stores. THREE backends ship, differing by SHARING SCOPE. **In-memory** per namespace (zero config; lazy expiry plus an unref'd sweep, `sweepInterval` ms, default 30000) — SINGLE-PROCESS, lost on restart. **SQLite** (`core/connectors/sqlite/lib/kv-store.js`, #KV1 slice 2) — zero npm deps via the `lib/sqlite-driver` seam (node:sqlite, `bun:sqlite` adapter under Bun), DURABLE across restarts and shared across PROCESSES on ONE HOST; namespaces sharing a file are isolated by a composite `(ns, key)` primary key rather than a prefix, `clear()` is one namespace-scoped DELETE, and every read-modify-write verb runs inside `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`/`COMMIT` — the synchronous driver makes a verb indivisible only WITHIN a process, which is precisely the guarantee that fails once a second process opens the file, i.e. the reason to pick this backend at all. **Redis** — shared across HOSTS. **Redis** (`core/connectors/redis/lib/kv-store.js`, #KV1 slice 1): point a namespace's `store` at a `connectors.json` entry and the `lib/kv-store` dispatcher resolves `core/connectors/<connector>/lib/kv-store.js`; naming a connector that has none still REFUSES the boot rather than degrading silently to memory (the others arrive demand-first, the audit-store shipping order). The redis backend keeps every guarantee server-side: `SET .. PX .. NX` for setnx, `GETDEL` for consume when the server has it (>= 6.2) with a **Lua fallback below that — never a GET+DEL pair**, which would let two concurrent readers both redeem; Lua also for compare-and-delete and for TTL-on-CREATE-only counters (`n === by` is a racy proxy for "was created", so existence is checked inside the script). Keys are prefixed `kv:<namespace>:` by default, so two namespaces may share one entry; cluster prefixes are deliberately NOT hash-tagged (every KV op is single-key, and tagging would pin a namespace to one slot — the opposite of the job store, whose MULTI/SUNION/MGET require the tag), so `clear()` scans each master node and deletes per key rather than assuming one slot. Connection policy (`commandTimeout`/`maxRetriesPerRequest`/`enableOfflineQueue`) is passed through from the entry and otherwise left at ioredis's defaults — deliberately NOT the render-cache's fail-fast tuning, because the right policy depends on the namespace's `failMode`. Deliberate boundary — NOT a redis client: no data structures (lists/hashes/sets/streams/pub-sub), no batch `mget`/`mset`, no key scanning (use `clear()` or track your own keys), no binary values (the storage layer owns bytes), no first-class distributed locks (compose `setnx` + `delIfEquals`; a lock API done right needs fencing/renewal policy no half-primitive should imply). `lib/kv` is framework-independent (config, connector stores and the warn sink are injected by gna.js at boot; `test/lib/kv-import-boundary.test.js` enforces the boundary) and plain-require'd (its namespace registry and sweep timers survive dev-mode refreshCore). Server-side only — NOT browser-bundled, so pickup is a bundle RESTART, no re-bake.
315. **Rate limiting (#MS6) — identified-caller quotas at the router band.** Opt-in via settings.json `server.rateLimit` (`enabled` strictly true, `namespace`, `keyField`, `limit`, `window`; folded into the runtime server block with env.json keys winning, resolved once at engine start onto the instance, so changes need a bundle restart; structurally invalid values on an enabled block refuse the boot). QUOTA semantics, not flood control: the gate runs AFTER route authorization (`authorizeRequest` is the principal resolver — the only writer of `req.machineCaller`, and session identity is its predicate) and BEFORE DTO validation, so the order is 401 -> 429 -> the validation-tier 422s (message validation when declared, then DTO) and a throttled caller never receives a 422 field map. A request with NO resolvable principal is SKIPPED, never bucketed — anonymous flood control belongs to the edge proxy and the #H9 HTTP/2 rapid-reset guard, and IP-keying is dishonest behind a proxy (every socket.remoteAddress is the proxy's). Keys: `u:<session.user[keyField]>` for signed-in callers (the field is operator-named because session.user is app-owned shape; an absent/empty value means unidentified => skipped) and `m:<machineCaller.name>` for #MS3 machine callers; session wins, mirroring the authz gate; values over 180 chars are sha256-hexed under the kv 512-char key cap. Counters are FIXED WINDOWS over the #KV1 primitive — `incr(key, 1, {ttl: windowMs})`, TTL-on-create-only, race-free in all three backends — so choosing the namespace's backend chooses the quota's SCOPE: in-memory counts PER PROCESS (each replica grants the quota again; the resolver warns), redis/sqlite share across replicas/processes. For a redis-backed namespace set `enableOfflineQueue: false` + `commandTimeout` on the connectors entry (the render-cache L2 fail-fast trio; with ioredis defaults an outage QUEUES every gated request so neither failMode ever fires — the resolver warns about this too). Outage policy IS the namespace's `failMode`: `open` => incr degrades to null and the gate ALLOWS without headers (the explicit `count === null` check is load-bearing — `null <= limit` is true by coercion); `closed` => the rejection is owned and answers 503 + Retry-After (the caller is NOT over quota). Denials answer 429 via `controller.throwError` with Retry-After (from the store's own ttl — one extra read on the throttled path only) plus the draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers-11 structured fields (`RateLimit: "<policy>";r=<remaining>[;t=<sec>]`, `RateLimit-Policy: "<policy>";q=<limit>;w=<windowSec>`); allowed limited requests carry both without `t` (reporting it honestly would cost a second read per request and the parameter is optional). Per-route overrides are TOP-LEVEL routing.json keys (never under `param` — the #CSRF2 trap), propagated by BOTH route builders (cold typeof-guarded — `false` is meaningful — and the warm cached-route opt-in copy): `"rateLimit": false` exempts the route; `{limit, window}` REPLACES the default for that route in its OWN bucket (`<principal>:<rule>`), partial objects inherit the missing key; shapes are linted at boot (a malformed value refuses the boot — the DTO registrar doctrine). Dormant => the dispatch band runs today's exact synchronous path with ZERO promises minted; armed, every terminal of the verdict promise is owned (allow -> band, deny/outage -> answered inside the gate) so a store failure can never strand a request. Implementation: `lib/rate-limit` (plain-required, router-bound), wired in `core/router.js` at both dispatch sites; server-side only, but the route-flag propagation lives in browser-bundled `lib/routing`, so the release carries a dist rebuild (dead code client-side). Tests: `test/core/rate-limit.test.js` (45 — source pins on every seam, resolver refusal/warn matrix, gate behaviour over a scripted namespace, 5 mutation controls fired red-first).
316. **Reserved-action controller hooks (`onReady`, `setup`) — dispatch semantics + the #B399 ownership guard** — Before the main action, `core/router.js` dispatches the two reserved hooks at BOTH dispatch sites (with- and without-middleware), in order, synchronously, without awaiting: an app defines `this.onReady = function(req, res, next){...}` on the controller, and `setup` resolves through a framework-synthesized wrapper that requires the bundle's `controllers/setup.js` once per controller instance (the wrapper returns the app call's own result). Since #B399, both hook loops run INSIDE the dispatch try and each hook's return value is captured — a thenable gets a `.catch` routing to `throwError(response, 500, ...)` naming the failing hook, the same guard shape the main action dispatch carries. Consequences: a SYNC hook throw answers 500 (previously it escaped to process level — on the built-in engine that was uncaughtException → emerg + SIGTERM, killing the whole bundle; Express's layer-catch answered its own 500 — engine-asymmetric); an ASYNC hook rejection answers 500 when it lands before the response is released, and degrades to the #ERRREF pairing log line when the action already responded (`throwError` is `!headersSent`-guarded). Ordering caveat: hooks are dispatched in the same synchronous frame as the action (never awaited), so a rejecting async hook does NOT prevent the action from running — its side effects still execute even when the wire answers 500; hooks are not a gating mechanism (use route middleware, route authorization, or DTO validation to refuse a request before the action). Sync or absent hooks mint zero promises — dispatch timing is unchanged for every controller that does not return a thenable from a hook. **The QUERY-DELIVERY half of the same #B399 arc (shipped separately): every app-callback delivery in `Controller::query()`** — the Node-style callback form and the `{onComplete}` facade, both transports, success/status AND transport-error deliveries — routes an `async` callback's rejected promise through one constructor-scope `_ownAsyncCbRejection` helper to the same throwError(500) shape the sync-delivery catches build (marker: `Controller Query Exception on async callback rejection.`). Pre-fix the rejection floated to the process handler and the request hung; the two success-delivery sync catches are byte-unchanged, plain callbacks mint zero promises, and a callback that responded before rejecting is absorbed by the #B31 released-response guard. The SYNC half of the same error-path surface is owned too (#B402): all 14 formerly-bare transport-error deliveries (host-missing, circuit refusal, the query-scope outer catch, both ca-read catches, h1 ALPN/request-error, the h2 typed terminals and both pre-flight PING failures) wrap the callback in try/catch routing to a shared `_ownSyncCbThrow` guard (marker: `Controller Query Exception on transport-error callback throw.`, flat 500) — previously an event/timer-frame throw escaped to the process handler (lib/proc.js: emerg + SIGTERM, a whole-bundle kill on BOTH engines for consumer bundles, since an app bug's error code matches none of the transport-lifecycle survive branches), and the caller-frame sites re-invoked the app callback a second time through the query-scope catch, handing it its own exception as the query error. The h2 session-error handler no longer answers the request itself (#B403): request notification on a failing session is owned solely by the stream-level typed deliveries (every live stream self-delivers), retiring the session-level throwError that raced the app callback's own response — and that, on a REUSED session, could answer with the CREATING request's context (session listeners bind once at fresh connect; the cache-hit path never re-binds them). Its by-catch #B404 is FIXED in the same pending release: every error-path `query#complete` emit is SINGLE-argument (mirroring the callback form — `callback(err)` on failure), while both `onComplete` facades' `(err, data)` dispatch dereferenced `data.status` unconditionally — so in handle/emitter mode a transport error or non-2xx outcome never reached the app's listener and the request answered 500 through the facade's sync catch with a marker misattributing it to an app callback exception. A `typeof data == 'undefined'` guard opening each facade's sync-guard try now delivers the payload as the error argument (on failure `cb(err)` with `data` undefined — a plain `{status, error}` object for a non-2xx status or a transport failure, a native `Error` for a pre-transport failure (missing host, unreadable certificate, open circuit) — and on success `cb(false, data)`); listener sync throws and async rejections are owned like every other delivery — and the host-missing emitter branch gained the `return` its callback twin always had (the only fall-through of the 20 emit sites — all 20 of which, with the probe-release branch, were removed by the #B475 cleanup commit of 2026-09-05 once `query()` always supplied a callback; the event now fires only from `query()`'s one-tick fallback). The documented `util.promisify(self.query)` idiom always used the callback form and was never affected by #B404 — but WAS broken by the last divergent cell, retired as #B405 (measured with controls in both directions): the h2 CALLBACK-mode dispatch delivered only 5xx to the callback and answered every other deliverable non-2xx itself via throwError, so h2 graceful degradation was impossible for 4xx and a promisified h2 query NEVER SETTLED on any non-5xx status (the await's continuation silently abandoned). Every body-announced non-2xx with a known status code now invokes `callback(data)` on both transports (h1 has done this since its #Q1 change, whose inline comment states the intent; the 3xx-with-headers replay is untouched; the retired split is preserved as comments at the site), so the promisify rejection contract now holds transport-uniformly.
317. **Boot-frame failure ownership — a crash during bundle bootstrap aborts loudly instead of hanging (#B406, 2026-08-23).** `core/gna.js`'s boot callback (`onGettingProjectConfig`) is declared `async`, so a synchronous throw anywhere in its ~1470-line direct frame became a promise REJECTION: the caller's try/catch (written for a plain callback) could never see it, and the process-level `unhandledRejection` net only logs at error level — no `[ emerg` marker, no exit. The daemon's startup watchdog (`lib/cmd/bundle/start.js`) reads the child's STDOUT only, during startup only, and matches `/(\[|\[\s+)emerg/` — on a match it SIGKILLs the child, prints the cause, and clears the startup timer; a child that dies WITHOUT the marker gets the immediate exit-code report; a child that neither exits nor emits the marker got the 60-second timeout with no cause. Pre-fix, a boot crash in that frame was the third shape. The whole frame is now owned by one try/catch routing every failure — sync throws today, any awaited rejection added later — into `abort()`, the existing boot terminal (context-aware `console.emerg` + synchronous `fs.writeSync(2)` flush + `process.exit(1)`), with non-Error rejections (`throw null`) coerced to an Error FIRST because `abort()` reads `.stack` through branches that would themselves throw on null — and a throw inside the catch would escape back to the silent net. Measured: the levelled emerg line SURVIVES an immediate `process.exit(1)` on a POSIX pipe (short writes; the 64KB truncation class is large payloads), so the single marker line reaches the watchdog — deliberately ONE marker-bearing line, since the watchdog's emerg branch has no re-entry guard and two lines risk double-firing its bulk-start accounting. Behaviour change: a throw LATE in the frame that previously left a half-initialised process limping now refuses the boot. Extends entry 178's severity-axis rule ("lethality follows the nearest async boundary") with the boot-time tier: at boot there is no request to degrade to a logged rejection — an unowned rejection means the process neither starts nor exits, which is strictly worse than either crash-and-respawn or a 500. Tests: `test/core/gna-boot-frame-ownership.test.js` (source pins red-first vs the pre-fix blob; replica arms incl. an awaited-rejection arm proving the seam is ready for a boot-time `await`, a child-process SUBTRACT reproducing the pre-fix escape at a real process-level net, and a plain-callback CONTROL locking the caller contract). Server-side only: pickup is a bundle restart, no re-bake.


318. **Validator AJAX bodies are JSON — the Content-Type must say so, on every sender (#FORMCT; query path fixed in #B425).** The browser validator serializes its request bodies with `JSON.stringify`, but its shared `xhrOptions` defaults hardcode `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded; charset=UTF-8` (that literal appears exactly once in the whole shipped bundle). When a JSON body goes out under that label the gina server correctly honours it and runs `body.replace(/\+/g, ' ')` plus `decodeURIComponent` BEFORE `JSON.parse` — so a value such as an email `+alias` arrives with the `+` turned into a space. **The failure is silent by construction:** the mangled body is still well-formed JSON, so it parses, no error is raised, and the endpoint answers `200` with a wrong answer. The server half is NOT the bug — for a genuine urlencoded body `+` really does mean space and `%2B` survives the decode — so every fix belongs on the client, at the labelling. **Rule for any new sender: if the body is JSON, resolve the Content-Type as `explicit author declaration, else application/json` — never let the urlencoded default ride a JSON body.** The senders and their state: the form-submit non-binary path and the file-removal POST resolve it correctly (they read an explicit form `enctype` first, else `application/json`); the multipart/binary path sets its own boundary header; a bodiless branch sets a header but sends nothing, so nothing can be corrupted; and the `query` (live-check) request in `core/plugins/lib/validator/src/form-validator.js` was the last one still inheriting the default — fixed by mirroring the same resolution. **Implementation gotcha specific to the query path:** the rule author can override the header per rule (`"headers": { "Content-Type": "application/json" }` inside a rule's `query` block, a supported seam), and that override must keep winning — but the options merge folds the rule block and the defaults into one object, after which a rule-declared `urlencoded` and the inherited default are the same string in the same slot. Provenance is unrecoverable post-merge, so the rule-declared value must be captured BEFORE the merge and consulted afterwards. **Behaviour note at pickup:** live-check bodies now route to the server's parse-verbatim JSON branch, so `+` survives — and `%XX` sequences are no longer URL-decoded either. The client stringifies raw field values without percent-encoding, so no correct consumer depends on that decode, but a bundle that leaned on it will see the literal. **Merge semantics this relies on (measured, and undocumented in the merge JSDoc):** `lib/merge` is variadic — it reads `override` off the LAST argument only when that argument is a boolean, and treats every other argument as an additional source, with EARLIER sources winning and later ones filling gaps. That is why a per-rule header beats the default, and why passing a third object is a merge rather than an override flag.
319. **Controller render data — the dotted-path `set()` contract, and why a first write must never be walked (#P39 slice 2).** Inside `core/controller/controller.js`, every render is preceded by ~60 calls to a local `set('a.b.c', value)` that builds `local.userData` (`page.view.*`, `page.environment.*`, `page.forms`, `gina.csrfToken`, …). Its contract: missing intermediates are created as plain objects and an intermediate that is not a plain object (`null`, an array, a primitive) is REPLACED; at the leaf, **first write wins** (a later `set()` to an existing leaf is ignored — the `override` argument is accepted but inert), an object written onto an existing object leaf **deep-fills** it (missing keys added, existing kept) through `lib/merge`, and **a first-write value is stored by reference and is never walked, copied or mutated**. That last clause is the load-bearing one: `set('page.forms', conf.content.forms)` stores the shared per-process forms catalog, and the previous implementation — a JSON-string path builder + `JSON.parse` + a whole-subtree `merge` — recursed into every grafted object, re-merged each array inside it with itself, and wrote the copies back into the caller's object: 0.4–1.5 ms of CPU per request for a real catalog, and the catalog's arrays silently swapped for equal copies on every render. (That lib-level rewrite of a grafted source — array identity churn at every depth plus SILENT PRIMITIVE DEDUPE — was #B428, fixed in 0.6.19: `lib/merge` now skips a subtree that is the SAME object on both sides — merging a value into itself is identity — so a grafted source keeps its arrays and duplicates and the result references it; object/array references only, equal primitives keep their path; the root-absent `createMode` shallow-copy path is deliberately unchanged. Measured on a 2000-case seeded corpus: identical results and untouched sources for every non-shared merge. Two by-catches were staked out of it: #B436 — FIXED in 0.6.20: staked as 'nested arrays at depth ≥ 2 merge TWICE' (`[1,2,3,4,3,4]`), the MEASURED root was `mergeArray`'s number top-up deciding 'push again' by INDEX rather than by COUNT — any number the target already held at a shifted index was pushed again at EVERY depth (`merge([9,1],[1])` → `[9,1,1]`; `{ports:[8080,8124]}`+`{ports:[8124]}` → `[8080,8124,8124]`), and the depth-≥2 double pass (`browse()` merged arrays in its prop loop and again in the recursion) merely manufactured the shift; the top-up now compares counts (`[25]`+`[25,25]` still `[25,25]`, a present value is never pushed again, merging the same source twice is a no-op) and the prop-loop array merge runs only on the createMode path, so a nested array is merged once and an array SHARED by both sides at depth ≥ 2 keeps its identity (a #B428 residual); #B437 — FIXED in 0.6.20: a target array repeating a primitive (`['v2','v2']`) merged with an array of objects threw `TypeError: Cannot create property 'id' on string`, because `mergeArray`'s object-fill branch tested for a free index on the DEDUPED rebuild of the target and then wrote into the real target, whose index still held the string (or `null`); an occupied index is now left alone, as it already was for an object landing on one.) The rewrite assigns a first write directly and routes only genuine collisions through `merge` at the leaf, so the observable structure is identical (11,550 states differential-tested against the frozen old implementation) while the catalog is left alone; measured ×4.5 on the primitive writes and ×800+ on the catalog write. **Two generalisable traps from that work.** (1) Until 0.6.19 `lib/merge` MUTATED A SOURCE IT GRAFTED: a source subtree grafted by reference at an existing level was walked by the recursion with `src === copy`, every array inside it re-merged with itself and the copies written back into the caller's object — contents preserved, identity churned, cost proportional to the value. #B428's identity guard closed it, and the lesson stands for any merge-like helper that walks a caller's object by reference: measure identity through it before handing it an object you must keep intact. (2) `lib/merge` is VARIADIC and its copy behaviour depends on depth and shape: a value at depth 1 of a call is shallow-copied, deeper values are referenced (and until 0.6.20 a nested array was merged twice on the same level — once in the graft loop, once in the recursion). The array contract is now in its JSDoc (#B436); still read `browse()` before reasoning about identity through merge, and prefer a measured differential test over a model of it.
320. **`route.request()` settles its caller exactly once - an outbound-request failure is an error argument, never a hang and never a bundle kill (#B442, 0.6.21).** The routing helper's outbound call (`getRoute(...).request([ignoreWebRoot,] options[, cb])`) DISCARDED the `ClientRequest` returned by `http(s).get`, so nothing could ever attach an `'error'` listener to it. Three consequences, all removed: (a) a dial failure whose code is carved out of the process-level uncaughtException handler (`ECONNREFUSED`/`ECONNRESET`/`EPIPE`/...) left the caller waiting FOREVER with nothing logged - a permanent wedge in any serialized consumer (a worker at concurrency 1, a queue processor), and the SILENCE is the defect, not the carve-out; (b) a code that is NOT carved out (`ETIMEDOUT`, `EHOSTUNREACH`, `ENETUNREACH` - i.e. a peer that stops answering or a route that goes away) escalated to `uncaughtException` and took the bundle down through the process-level `dismiss(pid, 'SIGTERM')`; (c) a response stream dying mid-body assigned its error to a local and waited for an `'end'` event that never arrives, so the assigned error was never delivered either. All four exit paths now run through ONE single-settle latch (`settled` flag + `settle()`), so the callback receives an ordinary error argument - the shape consuming code already handles - and can never be invoked twice. **`options.timeout` was INERT and looked like a consumer workaround:** it does reach `http(s).get`, but Node only EMITS `'timeout'` and never destroys the socket, and the request object was unreachable, so nobody could listen or act. It is now honoured - on expiry the request is destroyed and the callback settles with an `Error` carrying `code === 'ETIMEDOUT'`; absent/falsy `options.timeout` attaches no timeout listener, so the behaviour is opt-in. The no-callback (fire-and-forget) branch attaches its own `'error'` listener and `console.warn`s, so a call nobody awaited can no longer kill the process. Same defect class as the `store()` / `copyFile` movers (#B223/#B227): capture every request or stream you create, listen on BOTH ends, and latch the settle. **`lib/routing` IS browser-bundled** (aliased in the plugin `build.json`), so this ships in `gina.min.js` as well as server-side - pickup is a bundle restart AND a re-bake. Regression test: `test/lib/routing-request-settle.test.js` - source pins plus extract-and-execute behavioural arms driving the real shipped bytes against a fake agent; note the function region is brace-UNBALANCED (a `/^\{/` regex literal in the end handler), so the extraction is terminator-anchored on `} // EO route.request()` and a brace walker must NOT be substituted for it.
321. **`merge()` array-element hardening - a null (or hole) element in an id-keyed array is an element with no key, never a crash (#B436/#B437/#B443 arc).** `typeof null == 'object'`, so `mergeArray`'s collection paths historically dereferenced null elements and threw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null` - and because every configuration overlay and collection merge travels through `lib/merge`, any such shape was a whole-merge (often whole-boot) kill. The hardened contract, in layers: the WRITE side (0.6.20) - the index-merge branch tests for a free slot on the real target, and an occupied slot (a primitive or null left where the deduped rebuild had a hole) is skipped, never written into; number top-up is by COUNT, not index, so merges are idempotent (`[25]+[25,25]` gives `[25,25]`, `[9,1]+[1]` stays `[9,1]`). The READ side (0.6.21) - both collection ENTRY guards null-check the TARGET operand (they already checked the source), both id-ROSTER loops and both WALKS skip a null element, and the per-element collection tests null-check the SOURCE operand; a null element matches nothing, blocks nothing and contributes nothing. Semantics otherwise unchanged and pinned: a target whose slots are primitives/null keeps them (`[null,null]+[{id:1},{id:2}]` returns `[null,null]`, same as `['v2','v2']+...`), and an object BEHIND a primitive/null head is dropped by the per-element branch (pre-existing, `['x',{id:9}]+[{id:1}]` returns `['x']`). `lib/merge` is browser-bundled (aliased in the plugin `build.json`), so array-merge fixes ship in `gina.min.js` too - pickup is a bundle restart AND a re-bake. Regression suites: `test/lib/merge-b436.test.js`, `merge-b437.test.js`, `merge-b443.test.js` (behavioural arms driving the real lib + comment-stripped source pins + artifact-derived dist pins, all red-first validated). **#B446 — the same `for...in` loops are also a prototype-pollution sink.** `merge()` enumerated SOURCE keys with bare `for...in` at five sites (`:136`, `:197`, `:208`, `:237`, `:547` pre-fix; the lone `hasOwnProperty` at `:548` guards the TARGET, not the source), so an OWN `__proto__` key — exactly what `JSON.parse` yields, and what `core/server.js:6657` feeds it on the PUT path — walked through to `Object.prototype`. ⚠️ Subtler still: merge reads `src = target[name]` THROUGH the prototype chain, so with its documented target-wins-on-conflict rule a polluted value BEAT a default the source literal owned (measured: `rejectUnauthorized` flipping true→false on the query-options defaults). All five loops now reject `__proto__`/`constructor`/`prototype` BY NAME — that name check is the whole guard, and it is REQUIRED because own-property checking alone cannot see a JSON-parsed `__proto__` (an own key satisfies an own check by construction). ⚠️ The first cut ALSO skipped non-own keys as extra hardening and that was REVERTED before release: the model layer round-trips entity instances through `merge()` — the in-tree path is the relations assembly (`core/model/entity.js`); the registry's `setModel` (`lib/model.js`) has no in-tree caller but is published through the `modelUtil` context and stays consumer-reachable — and all six SQL connectors attach their `.sql`-derived query methods to the PROTOTYPE, so own-only copying silently dropped every query method (`db.<x>Entity.getOneById is not a function`) while constructor-assigned methods survived — a partial, hard-to-attribute breakage caught by a consumer on the unpublished tree, never shipped. `merge()` walks the prototype chain, as it always has; only the three key names are refused. Regression suite: `test/lib/merge-entity-prototype.test.js` (red-first validated against the own-guard build). The `src`-read is deliberately left prototype-reachable — closing it would change documented conflict semantics for objects that legitimately inherit, and is tracked separately. **#B450 — the plain-object check itself CRASHED on shadowed `constructor` keys (pre-existing, measured identical on shipped 0.6.21).** `isObject()`'s eager `hasMethodPrototyped` compute (a "node > v6" edit that broke jQuery isPlainObject's short-circuit) read `.prototype` off an OWN `constructor` value, so `{"job":{"constructor":<primitive|null|{}|[]>}}` — FIVE measured shapes — threw `Cannot convert undefined or null to object` from any PUT body BEFORE the key filter could drop the name (the guard rejects keys at COPY time; this crash fired in the type predicate deciding recursion, one level up). Fixed by restoring the lazy short-circuit and guarding the `.prototype` read; a 24-shape differential sweep pins IDENTICAL answers on every input the old form did not crash on — so the recurse-vs-graft routing (plain objects recurse into fresh clones; class instances and functions graft by REFERENCE, which config singletons and instance registries rely on) is unchanged, and every crash shape now yields the disclosed drop-the-key behaviour with sibling fields surviving. Regression suite: `test/lib/merge-b450.test.js` (red-first: the five crash arms + boolean sibling fail on the pre-fix predicate; pollution/entity/graft controls green on both revisions).
322. **OWASP Top 10 response — framework-side security headers, request-body bounds, opt-in SRI (#OW1/#OW2/#OW3, 0.6.23).** Three framework-layer hardenings shipped together. **#OW1 headers:** `settings.json > server.securityHeaders` — the framework itself emits security headers on BOTH engines, because the #HDR plugins are express middleware and the default isaac engine never runs the express chain for HTTP responses (`server.use` middlewares are only ever drained by the WebSocket session binder against an inert response), so a mounted `SecurityHeaders()` orchestrator emitted NOTHING there; the emitter (`lib/security-headers-emitter`) is the framework-side twin of the #HDR8 hidePoweredBy gate. Tier A on by default (cannot break a working app): x-content-type-options / x-download-options / x-permitted-cross-domain-policies / x-xss-protection / referrer-policy / x-dns-prefetch-control / origin-agent-cluster. Tier B opt-in, one key each, each with a NAMED breakage: xFrameOptions (cross-origin embedding) / coop (severs window.opener — OAuth/payment popups) / corp (conflicts with gina's own `access-control-allow-origin: *` on `/_gina/*`) / hsts (180-day commitment, emitted over http too). First-writer-wins (a mounted plugin / `env.json` header / upstream proxy beats the framework default); coop/corp never applied to `/_gina/*`; header VALUES are asserted in tests against each plugin's own exported constant so framework and mounted plugin cannot diverge; `server.hidePoweredBy` default flipped to `true` (note the render-cache interaction: with the cache enabled and `server.cache.name` unset, the boot warning about `Cache-Status` still naming the framework fires — set a token there). `server.securityHeaders.enabled: false` restores the previous behaviour. **#OW2 body bounds:** `server.maxBodySize` (`"64MB"`, ENFORCED: 413 + `request.destroy()`, plus a `_bodyRejected` guard on the `end` handler because destroy racing buffered chunks would otherwise double-respond) and `server.maxBodySizeWarn` (`"2MB"`, warn-only) bound non-multipart bodies counting RAW wire bytes (a multi-byte UTF-8 body is larger on the wire than its decoded string length); `0` disables either; B/KB/MB/GB accepted (bare number = MB); multipart stays under the `upload.*` caps; `server.timeout` is exposed and defaults to `0` DELIBERATELY — a finite whole-request clock kills SSE/WebSocket, and the slow-body case is closed by the cap. **#OW3 SRI:** `templates.json > "_common" > "sriEnabled": true` (default false, bare boolean per that file's `*Enabled` convention) makes the controller's resource builder add ` integrity="sha384-..." crossorigin="anonymous"` to same-origin `<script>` AND `<link rel=stylesheet>` tags whose files resolve on disk — including `gina.min.js`/`gina.min.css`, which ride the framework conf's `_common` collections through the same emission path. `lib/sri` is FAIL-OPEN always (external `://` and protocol-relative `//` URLs, unresolvable paths, unreadable files, missing conf → NO attribute, never a guess — an absent attribute loads as before, a wrong one hard-blocks); resolution = query/fragment strip → webroot un-prefix → `content.statics[url]` exact match → `publicPath + url` (directory-mapped statics resolve nowhere → fail-open, deliberate); the hash cache is STAT-VALIDATED (mtimeMs + size, one statSync per lookup) so a rebuilt/re-baked asset re-hashes on the next render with NO restart — but pages already stored by the render/output cache keep the hash they were rendered with, so flush that cache after an asset rebuild; the HTTP/2 preload hint is SUPPRESSED for SRI'd assets (a hint carries no integrity metadata — a mismatched preload is a wasted double-fetch); sha384 is HARDCODED as a measured safety property (48-byte digest → 64 base64 chars, ZERO `=` padding, keeping integrity values structurally inert to the asset catalog's unanchored `(src|href|srcset)=` scan — sha512's padded base64 would reopen that hazard, so no algorithm knob ships); coverage caveats, both fail-safe: popin re-creates injected scripts copying only `src` (SRI not enforced on popin-injected loads) and the client loader's dynamic gina.min.css injection is likewise uncovered. Pickup: all three are server-side — bundle restart, no dist rebuild (`lib/sri` is not browser-bundled).
323. **Exact-money primitive — `lib.money` / `gina.money` (#FIN5).** Monetary amounts must never ride IEEE-754 floats (`0.10 + 0.20` is wrong out of the box); the money module makes the correct pattern cheap: amounts travel as STRINGS on the wire (the JSON parser preserves them byte-exact), live as INTEGER minor units (BigInt) internally, and only become locale display via `Intl.NumberFormat` (the i18n layer's job — deliberately NOT this module's). API, identical server-side (`require('lib/money')` bare-module or `lib.money`) and client-side (`gina.money`, browser-bundled): `parse(str, code)` — strict wire-string parse that THROWS on a number input, a malformed string, or MORE fractional digits than the currency's exponent (rounding is the application's decision, never the library's); `fromMinor(int, code)` / `toMinor(a)` (JSON-safe string out); `add` / `subtract` / `compare` — same-currency ONLY, a mismatch always throws (mixed-currency arithmetic is the corruption class the module exists to prevent); `multiply(a, factor)` — INTEGER factors only (a fractional rate needs the application's own rounding, on minor units); `format(a)` — the canonical wire string with exactly the currency's fraction digits ('20.00', '-0.05', '150' for JPY); `exponent(code)` — ISO 4217 minor-unit exponent, default 2 with the exceptions in-lib (JPY/CLP/KRW/XOF… 0; BHD/KWD/OMR/TND… 3; CLF/UYW 4), malformed codes throw. Amount shape: `{ currency, exponent, minor: BigInt }` — exact beyond `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` minor units. The module is dependency-free, dual-published (node + AMD), and uses the `BigInt()` constructor form exclusively — no BigInt literals — so every tool in the browser-bundle build chain parses it. Pickup for changes: bundle restart AND re-bake (browser-bundled via build.json).

324. **Idempotency keys (#FIN6) — `Idempotency-Key` request deduplication at the router band, per the IETF draft (draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header).** Opt-in TWICE: settings.json `server.idempotency` (`enabled` strictly true + `namespace` naming a DECLARED kv namespace + `keyField` naming the session.user identity property; optional `ttl` default 24h, `inflightTtl` default 2m, `maxBodySize` default 256KB, `retryAfter` default 5s — folded from settings into the runtime server block with env.json winning, resolved once at engine start onto `instance._idempotency`, boot-REFUSED on a structurally invalid enabled block) AND per route: routing.json top-level `idempotency: true` or `{"required": true}` (400 when the header is missing) — top-level like `rateLimit`, NOT `param.*`; unflagged routes are byte-identical. Band order: 401 -> 429 -> idempotency (the gate runs strictly AFTER the rate-limit verdict at BOTH router dispatch sites, owned promise terminals) -> message validation (#FIN3, routes that declare it) -> DTO 422. Mechanics over the #KV1 primitive: the first request bearing a key RESERVES with `setnx` + the in-flight TTL (crash-safe by expiry: a dead process's reservation self-releases and a retry re-executes), executes with `request._idemCapture` stamped; `renderJSON` records the envelope at its single stringify choke point — status, ALLOWLISTED headers only (`content-type`, `location`; `set-cookie` is NEVER stored), body <= maxBodySize, sha256 payload fingerprint (verbatim `req.rawBody` when present, else the JSON-serialized parsed body) — under the retention TTL. A retry with the same key + payload is answered with the RECORDED response + `Idempotency-Replayed: true`; an in-flight duplicate gets 409 + Retry-After; the same key with a DIFFERENT payload gets 422; responses >= 500, oversize bodies, and anything not passing through renderJSON (a template render, a redirect, an error egress) RELEASE the reservation via the response-finish belt so retries re-execute — only what was recorded is ever replayed. Principal scoping is structural: the reservation key is `idem:<u:|m: principal>:<METHOD>:<rule>:<sha256 key>` (the rate-limit `deriveKey` precedence), so a stored response can never cross principals, and anonymous (principal-less) callers are SKIPPED entirely — the same class of lesson as the authz+cache replay hazard. Dedup SCOPE follows the namespace's backend: in-memory dedups PER PROCESS (a retry on another replica RE-EXECUTES — the resolver warns), redis/sqlite share across replicas. Outage policy is the namespace's `failMode`: `open` proceeds without dedup, `closed` answers 503 + Retry-After. Audit auto-events fire on the 400/409/422/503 denials. `lib/routing`'s per-route flag propagation rides the browser bundle (inert client-side — dist moves; the feature's pickup is a bundle restart). Tests: `test/core/idempotency.test.js` (48 — resolver matrix, gate verdicts, record/release, real kv memory-namespace round-trips).
325. **`renderXML` delegate (#FIN2) — first-class XML responses, the outbound half of #FIN1's verbatim inbound handling.** `self.renderXML(xmlContent[, contentType])` delegates to `core/controller/controller.render-xml.js` through the house delegate-to-file pattern (3-key deps `{self, local, headersSent}`, dev-mode `require.cache` bust). gina does NOT build XML any more than it parses it: the caller serialises with its own library and hands over a string; the delegate owns the wire concerns only. **Content-type defaults to `application/xml`** — RFC 7303 §4.1 recommends it over `text/xml`, and the mime table CANNOT supply it: `core/mime.types` declares the `xml` key TWICE (`:672` `application/xml`, `:673` `text/xml`), so JSON.parse last-wins resolves `mime['xml']` to `text/xml` (MEASURED). The duplicate is deliberately left alone — that key also types `.xml` STATICS, a separate blast radius.
